content: Since the last Cochrane Review in 2016, there has been ongoing debate about whether vitamin D can help reduce asthma exacerbations and improve asthma control. This updated meta-analysis includes data from new trials conducted since that time. The objective of this review was to assess the effectiveness and safety of vitamin D or its hydroxylated metabolites in reducing the risk of severe asthma exacerbations, defined as those requiring systemic corticosteroids, and in improving asthma symptom control. The researchers searched the Cochrane Airways Group Trial Register and reference lists of relevant articles. They also contacted study authors to identify additional trials. The last search was conducted on September 8, 2022. The review included double-blind, randomized, placebo-controlled trials involving children and adults with asthma. These trials evaluated the risk of asthma exacerbations, asthma symptom control, or both. Four authors independently applied inclusion criteria, extracted data, and assessed the risk of bias. Missing data were obtained from study authors when possible. Results were reported with 95% confidence intervals (CIs). The primary outcome was the incidence of severe asthma exacerbations requiring systemic corticosteroids. Secondary outcomes included asthma exacerbations leading to emergency department visits or hospitalizations, end-study Asthma Control Test (ACT) or childhood ACT (cACT) scores, and end-study percentage of predicted forced expiratory volume in one second (FEV1). Subgroup analyses were performed to explore whether the effects of vitamin D were influenced by baseline vitamin D levels, dose, dosing frequency, form of vitamin D, or participant age. The review included 20 studies: 15 trials with 1,155 children and 5 trials with 1,070 adults. Participant ages ranged from 1 to 84 years. Two trials focused on children under five years old (69 participants), and eight trials focused on children aged 5 to 16 years (766 participants). Across all trials, 1,245 participants were male, and 1,229 were female, with two studies not reporting sex distribution. Fifteen trials contributed data to the primary outcome analysis of exacerbations requiring systemic corticosteroids. Trial durations ranged from 3 to 40 months, and all but two trials investigated the effects of cholecalciferol (vitamin D3). Most participants had mild to moderate asthma, and profound vitamin D deficiency (25-hydroxyvitamin D < 25 nmol/L) at baseline was rare. The administration of vitamin D or its hydroxylated metabolites did not significantly reduce or increase the proportion of participants experiencing one or more asthma exacerbations requiring systemic corticosteroids (odds ratio [OR] 1.04, 95% CI 0.81 to 1.34; I² = 0%; 14 studies, 1,778 participants; high-quality evidence). This corresponds to an absolute risk of 226 per 1,000 participants in the vitamin D group compared to 219 per 1,000 in the placebo group. Vitamin D supplementation also had no effect on the rate of exacerbations requiring systemic corticosteroids (rate ratio 0.86, 95% CI 0.62 to 1.19; I² = 60%; 10 studies, 1,599 participants; high-quality evidence) or the time to the first exacerbation (hazard ratio 0.82, 95% CI 0.59 to 1.15; I² = 22%; 3 studies, 850 participants; high-quality evidence). Subgroup analyses did not show any evidence that baseline vitamin D levels, dose, dosing frequency, or participant age modified the effects of vitamin D supplementation. However, one trial investigating calcidiol (a hydroxylated form of vitamin D) reported a benefit for asthma control. Vitamin D supplementation did not affect any secondary efficacy outcomes, which were based on moderateor high-quality evidence. There was no effect on the incidence of serious adverse events (OR 0.89, 95% CI 0.56 to 1.41; I² = 0%; 12 studies, 1,556 participants; high-quality evidence). Fatal asthma exacerbations were not estimable, as no such events occurred in any trial. Six studies reported adverse reactions potentially related to vitamin D, including hypercalciuria, hypervitaminosis D, kidney stones, gastrointestinal symptoms, and mild itching. In one trial, the total number of participants with hypercalciuria could not be determined from the report. Three trials were assessed as having a high risk of bias in at least one domain, but none of these contributed data to the primary outcomes. Sensitivity analyses excluding these trials did not change the findings. In conclusion, this updated review does not support the use of vitamin D supplementation or its hydroxylated metabolites to reduce the risk of asthma exacerbations or improve asthma control. Participants with severe asthma and those with profound vitamin D deficiency were underrepresented in the included studies, so further research is needed in these populations. Additionally, the positive findings from a single study on calcidiol suggest that further investigation into this metabolite is warranted.
